{{Short description|Species of theropod dinosaur}} {{Speciesbox | fossil_range = [[Early Cretaceous]], {{fossilrange|Aptian|Aptian|early [[Aptian]]}} | image = Jian changmaensis (holotype, GSGM-D050).png | image_caption = Reconstruction of the known material on a silhouette (A) and photographs and line drawings of the holotype specimen (B–E) | display_parents = 2 | genus = Jian | parent_authority = Zhou et al., [[2026 in archosaur paleontology|2026]] | species = changmaensis | authority = Zhou et al., 2026 }} '''''Jian changmaensis''''' is an [[extinct]] species of [[microraptorine]] theropod dinosaur known from the [[Early Cretaceous]] ([[Aptian]] age) [[Xiagou Formation]] of China. ''J. changmaensis'' is the [[Monotypic taxon|only species]] in the genus '''''Jian''''', known from a [[pectoral girdle]] and partial forelimb. After the discovery of more than 100 bird fossils in the formation, this specimen is the first non-avian dinosaur to be described from it. == Discovery and naming == {{Location map|China | width = 225px | float = left | relief = yes | coordinates={{coord|39|51.32|N|96|46.77|E|display=inline}} | caption= ''J. changmaensis'' [[Type locality (biology)|type locality]] in Changma, China | pushpin_relief=1 }} The ''Jian'' fossil material was discovered in 2008 in outcrops of the [[Xiagou Formation]], part of the Changma Basin, near Changma village in northwest [[Gansu Province]], China. The specimen is housed in the Gansu Geological Museum, where it is permanently [[Accession number (cultural property)|accessioned]] as specimen GSGM-D050. It consists of an articulated portion of the skeleton, including the [[pectoral girdle]] ({{dinogloss|scapulocoracoid}}) and part of the forelimb ({{dinogloss|humerus}}, {{dinogloss|radius}}, and {{dinogloss|ulna}}). The specimen was initially reported in a 2010 [[conference abstract]]. In 2026, Ling-Qi Zhou and colleagues [[Species description|described]] ''Jian changmaensis'' as a new genus and species of microraptorine dinosaur based on these fossil remains, establishing GSGM-D050 as the [[holotype]] specimen. The [[Genus|generic name]], ''Jian'', references [[Biyiniao|Jiān]], a one-winged bird in Chinese legend. The [[Specific name (zoology)|specific name]], ''changmaensis'', references the [[Type locality (biology)|type locality]]. == Description == [[File:Jian changmaensis.png|thumb|[[Life restoration]]]] ''Jian'' is regarded as a medium-sized member of the Microraptorinae with a size in between that of ''[[Wulong bohaiensis|Wulong]]'' (known from an immature specimen), ''[[Zhongjianosaurus]]'', and small ''[[Microraptor]]'', and the larger ''[[Sinornithosaurus]]'' and ''[[Changyuraptor]]''. It is similar in size to large ''Microraptor'' specimens and a subadult specimen of ''Sinornithosaurus''. Based on the firm co-ossification of the elements of the pectoral girdle ({{dinogloss|scapula}} and {{dinogloss|coracoid}}, Zhou and colleagues identified the holotype as belonging to a skeletally mature individual. The lack of grooved and pitted textures on the bone surfaces also indicates it did not have the vascular canals seen in the bone of actively growing animals. [[Autapomorphies]] (unique derived characters distinguishing it from other species) of ''Jian changmaensis'' include the ratio of the coracoid to the humerus (greater than in any other microraptorine), the distal [[condyle]]s of the humerus primarily on the bone's cranial surface (in related species it is less cranially-oriented), and the presence of a prominent [[foramen]] at the top part of the radius when seen in [[Anatomical terms of location#Dorsal and ventral|ventral]] view (from below). == Palaeobiology == Several accumulations of shattered bird bones—reminiscent of the [[Pellet (ornithology)|pellets]] regurgitated by modern [[owl]]s—have been found in the Xiagou Formation site from which ''Jian'' is known. As the only non-bird from the locality, and as one of the largest known microraptorines, ''Jian'' may have been the producer of these bone masses. == Classification == To test the affinities and relationships of ''Jian'', Shou et al. (2026) included it in an updated version of the phylogenetic matrix of Pei et al. (2020). This analysis recovered ''Jian'' as a member of the [[dromaeosaurid]] subfamily [[Microraptorinae]]. Their 50% majority-rule consensus tree, which recovered better resolution than their strict consensus tree, placed it in an unresolved [[polytomy]] of [[Basal (phylogenetics)|derived]] microraptorines, including ''[[Hesperonychus]]'', ''[[Microraptor]]'', and ''[[Zhongjianosaurus]]''.
